Q59417261.summary: The Virgin sits enthroned as a queen, wearing the jewelled crown and pearl-studded robes of a Byzantine empress and holding a cross-staff, with the Christ Child seated upright on her lap in a purple robe; both wear golden haloes. Two haloed attendant figures, usually identified as angels, stand at either side. Darkened and worn, the great panel is one of the oldest surviving Marian icons in Rome, a witness to the city's devotion to Christ and his Mother in the early Middle Ages.
facts: Wikipedia notes that the icon is often linked with Pope John VII (705–707), whose kneeling figure is believed to appear, now very worn, at the Virgin's feet.
At about 164 × 116 cm it is the largest of the five oldest Marian icons in Rome.
Pope Alexander VII granted it a canonical coronation, which took place in 1659; it hangs above the altar of the Altemps Chapel.
Q59417261.notes: Date is debated (6th–9th century); association with John VII is common but not certain.

cur:manuscripts-paris-gregory-transfigur.summary: Christ stands in a pale mandorla on the summit of Mount Tabor between Elijah and Moses, his garments shining; below, Peter, James and John fall back on the rocky slope, shielding their eyes. The single full-page composition, with its gold-haloed figures against a blue ground, is one of the best preserved in the manuscript.
facts: The Paris Gregory was commissioned by Patriarch Photios as a gift for Emperor Basil I between 879 and 883 and is one of the most ambitious Byzantine manuscripts to survive from the generation after Iconoclasm.
Many of its full-page miniatures do not illustrate Gregory's sermons directly but set biblical and historical scenes beside them as a commentary devised for the court.
cur:manuscripts-paris-gregory-transfigur.notes: Folio derived from the Gallica image sequence (view number minus 13, halved) and checked against folios named on other Commons files of this manuscript; the Commons file name gives the Gallica view number, not the folio.

cur:manuscripts-utrecht-psalter-psalm-80.summary: Angels fly through the sky toward the Lord, who stands in an oval mandorla with a fluttering mantle, while below musicians blow long horns and play the psaltery and cithara, as the psalm commands: 'Sing aloud unto God our strength … blow up the trumpet in the new moon'.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm with a lively pen drawing that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its drawings are an important source for Carolingian musical instruments, which the artist labels in Latin.
cur:manuscripts-utrecht-psalter-psalm-80.notes: Detail of the drawing; the identification of the mandorla figure as the Lord follows the psalter's consistent iconography.

cur:manuscripts-cosmas-vat-gr-699-christ.summary: In a row of standing figures, each with a halo and named in Greek, Christ (labelled IC XC) stands second from the left holding a book, beside the Virgin, John the Baptist with a tall cross-staff, Zacharias with a censer, and Elizabeth; above, two medallions hold busts of Anna and Symeon. The group gathers the New Testament witnesses who first recognised the Messiah. This reproduction is in black and white.
facts: Wikipedia describes the Vatican copy as the earliest and best of the three nearly complete manuscripts of the Christian Topography, dating from the 9th century.
Cosmas, a 6th-century merchant who travelled as far as Sri Lanka, illustrated his treatise himself; the surviving manuscripts copy his drawings.
cur:manuscripts-cosmas-vat-gr-699-christ.notes: Black-and-white reproduction; identifications of the figures follow the Commons description (Virgin, Christ, John the Baptist, Zacharias, Elizabeth, Anna and Symeon).

cur:objects-clonmacnoise-cross-of-the-sc.summary: The west face of this magnificent cross centres on the Crucifixion, set in the ringed head, with further panels of the Passion on the shaft; on the east face Christ appears as Judge at the Last Judgment. Carved from fine sandstone, the figures are among the most accomplished of any Irish high cross. Displayed today in the visitor centre, it still conveys the monks' meditation on the whole drama of redemption.
facts: Wikipedia notes that its inscription asks for a prayer for Flann Sinna, King of Ireland, and Abbot Colmán, who commissioned it; it was carved around 900 and its panels include the Crucifixion, the Last Judgment and Christ in the Tomb.
The original was moved into the visitor centre in 1991 to protect it from the weather, and a replica stands on the original site.
